summary: Weekly POC sync focused on Dedicated sizing, autoscaling policy tradeoffs, and a planned burst test. Team aligned on actions: customer to share traffic shape; Redwood to propose autoscale runbook and run a burst test; pricing and SOW follow-up.

KV cache warmup and prefix caching
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Okay everyone, thanks for carving out time. We'll run 35, maybe 38 minutes. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Laura Kim: Laura here, Head of MLOps at CardioSense.
[00:10] Raj Patel: Raj, platform.
[00:12] Sofia Martinez: Sofia, product.
[00:14] Ethan Zhou: Ethan, dev.
[00:16] Diego Alvarez: Diego from Redwood, SE.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Priya, CSM.
[00:20] Jon Park: Jon, SRE.
[00:22] Maya Chen: Cool. Agenda: quick readout from last week's P50/P95 latency numbers, discuss autoscale policy knobs, plan a controlled burst test next week, and finalise what data you need to share.
[00:40] Raj Patel: Quick context — our traffic for the heartbeat-normalization endpoint is spiky: baseline 20 RPS, but we see short 90s of 800 RPS during report runs, roughly once every 6 hours.
[00:55] Laura Kim: And those bursts matter because downstream pipelines freeze if we miss more than ~10% of responses on those windows. So latency SLOs are strict.
[01:10] Diego Alvarez: Got it. From the POC side we measured median 45ms at baseline for the model variant you requested, P95 around 210ms when batching is on. But when we hit a synthetic burst we saw queuing creep up — that was before we wired autoscale policies.
[01:35] Ethan Zhou: When you say batching is on, is that continuous batching? How do you handle realtime tails?
[01:45] Diego Alvarez: We do continuous batching with an adaptive window; for low QPS it waits a short microwindow to form small batches, for high QPS it goes to large batches. There is an explicit max_batch_size config — we suggested 64 for your model initially.
[02:05] Sofia Martinez: Is there a tradeoff where bigger batches hurt tail latency?
[02:10] Diego Alvarez: Yes, larger batches increase per-batch throughput but can add scheduling latency for the first token in a micro-batch. That's why autoscaling + cache warmup are important: scale fast enough so batching operates in an efficient regime without pushing latency above your SLO.
[02:30] Priya Nair: Quick note — last week Maya sent a sizing table; customer asked for more concrete scale-up triggers.
[02:40] Maya Chen: Right, that's why Diego prepared some policy examples. Diego, can you walk through one?
[02:47] Diego Alvarez: Sure. Example A: aggressive scale-up. Trigger when 3-second moving average CPU/GPU utilization > 60% OR queue depth > 30 requests for two consecutive 30s intervals. Scale step: add 2 pods (or GPU workers) with a warmup grace of 45s, max burst workers capped at 6 above baseline. Scale-down: cooldown 180s after utilization below 30%. This keeps P95 tight during a burst but costs more.
[03:20] Raj Patel: What does "warmup grace" mean? Does that pre-warm KV cache?
[03:25] Diego Alvarez: Warmup grace is the policy that allows new workers to accept traffic but avoids immediate scale-down; it also triggers our KV cache prefetch hook if you provide prefix sets. It doesn't magically prepop cache unless you give warm prefixes — otherwise first requests to a new instance hit cold KV cache.
[03:45] Laura Kim: We have a set of common prefixes for yesterday's runs — can we feed those to pre-warm?
[03:50] Diego Alvarez: Absolutely. If you share a small list (1k keys) we can preload them during the burst test. That reduces cold-start tails.
[04:05] Sofia Martinez: For the SLOs — we are targeting P95 < 300ms and P99 < 600ms during bursts, is that realistic?
[04:14] Jon Park: Need to qualify: is that including queueing delay?
[04:18] Diego Alvarez: Our measurements typically include end-to-end server-side latency (queueing + GPU processing). For your model and quantization level, P95 below 300ms during a well-prepared burst is achievable if scaling is aggressive and cache is warmed. P99 at 600ms is a bit tight but possible with higher burst cap.
[04:38] Raj Patel: What's the cost delta if we bump the burst cap from +6 to +12?
[04:44] Maya Chen: Short answer: roughly linear for GPU-hour usage during burst windows. We'll produce a quick delta estimate in the SOW. Diego, can you add numbers?
[04:52] Diego Alvarez: I'll run the numbers: based on observed token/sec and batch sizes, doubling burst cap roughly doubles burst-hour spend. But we can also tune batch sizes and async prefetch to reduce cost.
[05:10] Ethan Zhou: Any fast wins to reduce cost while keeping latency?
[05:14] Diego Alvarez: Yes — prefix caching, model quantization (we're already on 4-bit variant?), and smarter routing: you can route non-latency-sensitive bulk jobs to a cheaper model variant during peaks. Also smaller max batch sizes for tail-critical routes.
[05:30] Laura Kim: We're using the medium quantized variant; we're open to testing lower precision if quality holds.
[05:36] Diego Alvarez: We'll add a QC eval to guard for quality regression.
[05:40] Maya Chen: Let's talk about the burst test plan. We proposed Wed next week, 16:00 PDT, 15 minutes of ramp, 5 minutes at peak, then cooldown. Is that still good for CardioSense?
[05:55] Laura Kim: Wed works but can we move it an hour earlier? We have an internal release at 17:30.
[05:59] Raj Patel: Earlier is fine; how about 14:30 PDT?
[06:03] Maya Chen: Sounds good. Diego, what's your exact test checklist?
[06:07] Diego Alvarez: Checklist: 1) Redwood sets baseline config and autoscale policy; 2) Customer provides traffic shape and prefix list; 3) Redwood runs dry-run locally to validate config; 4) Run burst from Redwood load generator to simulate QPS shape while streaming telemetry; 5) Customer observes and runs integration smoke tests; 6) Postmortem with traces and token-level cost. We'll also warm KV cache with supplied prefixes 5m prior.
[06:40] Sofia Martinez: If we run from Redwood's generator, how do we ensure it's representative? We have custom headers and user-identifiers that alter routing within our app.
[06:50] Diego Alvarez: Good point. We can replay a sanitized version of a production trace if you can provide it; otherwise we'll parameterize the generator with custom headers.
[07:02] Ethan Zhou: We can provide a 1-hour sampled trace and a transformation script to anonymize IDs.
[07:08] Raj Patel: Will Redwood need VPC access for the test?
[07:11] Jon Park: For Dedicated pilot currently in our managed environment, no VPC peering is required. If you want Private (VPC) then yes but that's a separate step.
[07:22] Laura Kim: We also care about graceful degradation — if capacity is exhausted, do you fallback to a cheaper model?
[07:28] Diego Alvarez: Yes, we can set routing policies: primary model, fallback model, and a per-route latency budget. If primary can't meet latency SLOs within X seconds, requests route to fallback. You can also set percent-based rollouts.
[07:40] Maya Chen: Any concerns on security or audit logs during the burst test?
[07:44] Priya Nair: We'll enable request-level logging but scrub tokens; we can also run with masked payloads. We will provide an audit log snapshot post-test.
[07:55] Sofia Martinez: On the topic of KV cache, what size would you allocate per worker?
[07:59] Diego Alvarez: Default is 2–4GB per worker for hot prefixes; depends on number of prefixes and expected token embeddings. We can scale that, but memory pressure affects eviction.
[08:10] Raj Patel: Are there limits for concurrent warmers during scale-up? If we prefetch a thousand keys across 10 workers, could that spike CPU?
[08:17] Diego Alvarez: It can. We recommend staged-prefetch: fan-out to new workers gradually, and throttle prefetch QPS. We'll script that in the runbook.
[08:30] Maya Chen: Let's pivot to SOW and pricing. Maya: do you want to summarize?
[08:35] Maya Chen: Sure. Post-burst test we'll provide: 1) findings doc, 2) updated autoscale runbook, 3) cost delta for different burst caps, 4) suggested policy defaults for 95th percentile and 99th percentile targets. We'll attach an SOW for a 3-week pilot extension if you choose to lock dedicated burst capacity.
[08:58] Laura Kim: The team will need estimated cost per peak-hour so finance can sign off.
[09:03] Maya Chen: We'll include a simple table: baseline hourly, burst hourly (+6 workers), burst hourly (+12 workers).
[09:10] Diego Alvarez: Also note there are mixed levers — you can reduce cost by 20–30% by combining prefix caching and a slightly higher baseline rather than big burst spikes; we'll model both.
[09:24] Raj Patel: About monitoring — can we get token-level cost and per-route latency dashboards during the run?
[09:30] Jon Park: Yes, Redwood Console will expose token breakdowns per model and route; we'll give you dashboard links and a shared playback of traces.
[09:40] Ethan Zhou: Are alerts supported in the POC? We want a Slack alert if P95>350ms for 1m.
[09:44] Priya Nair: Alerts can be configured in the Console; we'll provision an alert to your Slack channel during the test.
[09:50] Sofia Martinez: Quick question — is there any vendor lock-in if we use Redwood's Dedicated pool?
[09:55] Diego Alvarez: No vendor lock-in at the runtime level; models and configs are portable. The dedicated pool is subscription-based and we provide export tools for model artifacts and configs. Private deployments are available if you need on-prem.
[10:10] Laura Kim: One of our security folks asked about SOC 2 and KMS key control — do you have docs?
[10:14] Priya Nair: We'll resend the security pack (SOC2 report, KMS integration guide, SAML SSO docs).
[10:20] Raj Patel: Can you confirm audit logs retention window during the POC?
[10:24] Priya Nair: Default 30 days for the pilot; we can extend for an additional fee.
[10:30] Maya Chen: Back to autoscale knobs — Diego, can you enumerate the exact fields we'll put in runbook?
[10:36] Diego Alvarez: Yes: scale_up_trigger (utilization%, queue_depth), scale_step (workers), max_burst_workers, warmup_grace_seconds, scale_down_cooldown_seconds, min_replicas, max_replicas, prefetch_prefix_list (url), batch_max_size, batch_microwindow_ms. We'll include example values and tradeoffs.
[10:58] Raj Patel: For batch_microwindow_ms — is that something you tune per route?
[11:02] Diego Alvarez: Ideally yes; latency-sensitive routes get shorter microwindows. We'll recommend profile per route in the runbook.
[11:10] Laura Kim: For the burst test, do you recommend A/B comparing different policies?
[11:15] Diego Alvarez: We can run sequential tests: first conservative policy, then aggressive. Or run a synthetic A/B by splitting traffic 80/20 between policies — but that complicates analysis. Sequential runs are simpler.
[11:28] Sofia Martinez: Let's keep it sequential.
[11:31] Maya Chen: Any blockers to run on Wed 2025-09-17 at 14:30 PDT?
[11:36] Laura Kim: We need to export the traffic trace by 2025-09-11, so yes otherwise we'll reschedule.
[11:42] Maya Chen: Great. Quick clarifying Qs: Raj, you'll own trace export; Laura will own prefix list; Diego and Jon will own runbook and instrumentation; Maya will handle SOW and pricing.
[11:55] Raj Patel: Yep.
[11:56] Laura Kim: Yep.
[11:57] Diego Alvarez: I'll draft the runbook and share a high-level one pager ahead of the test.
[12:02] Priya Nair: We'll also set up a temporary Slack channel and add alert hooks.
[12:08] Maya Chen: Any last questions?
[12:12] Ethan Zhou: One nit — how do you measure cold-start impact versus queueing time in telemetry?
[12:18] Diego Alvarez: We emit markers: worker_start, prefetch_complete, first_token_latency; that lets us separate cold-start from queueing. We'll show a sample dashboard.
[12:30] Sofia Martinez: Good. If there are no more questions, let's recap next steps.
[12:34] Maya Chen: Recap: CardioSense to provide traffic trace (Raj) by 2025-09-11; prefix list (Laura) by 2025-09-11; Redwood to send autoscaling runbook and pricing delta by 2025-09-12; Diego to run burst test on 2025-09-17 14:30 PDT and stream telemetry; post-test readout within 48 hours.
[12:55] Laura Kim: Sounds good.
[12:57] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email and drop the runbook link.
[13:02] Diego Alvarez: Thanks, bye.
[13:04] (call ends)
